Blog   Customer Stories   Partner Program   Product Updates   Support   Startup Program   Sample Size Calculator   Statsig Lite   Statsig University. # Power and sample size: tools for experiment precision. Finding the optimal balance between power and sample size requires careful consideration of factors like the minimum detectable effect and the variance in the metric you're measuring. Tools like power analysis calculators can help figure out the necessary sample size for your desired level of power. Statsig’s platform makes this balancing act easier by providing built-in tools for power analysis and sample size calculations. With Statsig, you can design experiments that are both efficient and effective. Using power analysis tools, like **Statsig's Power Analysis Calculator**, helps determine the optimal experiment duration and the number of participants you need. Mastering the art of experimentation isn't just about the big picture—it's about fine-tuning the details like sample size, power, and data quality.

results.title: Rules of Thumb for Quantitative Experiments – Kromatic Blog
results.content: A lot of innovation work involves small sample sizes and relies on qualitative data. But eventually, we have to start running quantitative experiments, which requires a focus on quantitative experiment design. Watching or running countless quantitative experiments over the years, we’ve seen a lot of errors that come up time and time again. We don’t need a perfect experiment with 99.99967% confidence. We should think of each quantitative experiment like a minimum viable test and make sure we’re only gathering data that would tell us if we’re wrong. When we choose a metric, we should try thinking through the possible results. When trying to calculate the required sample size, don’t worry about getting the population size exactly right if it’s pretty large, e.g., 100,000 people. When the population is very large, the exact number doesn’t actually impact the sample size or margin of error. ### Decide on Sample Size. So pick the minimum sample size required for a margin of error that would potentially change your mind. When generating ideas during customer discoverer or usability testing, *Sample Size* should not be thought of in the same way as above. Don’t calculate margin of error with a different level than you agreed to when designing the experiment. Calculate the margin of error after the experiment, not before. (Try it using our experiment calculator. If you’re using a margin of error calculator that isn’t adjusting based on your result, it’s dead wrong.). And if running an A/B test, make sure you see margin of error on both sides of an A/B test. Special tip for investors and business managers: if a team is showing quantitative experiment results without a sample size or margin of error, you cannot judge the data. Try again and slowly increase the sample size. Don’t ignore your previous knowledge just because an A/B test tells you something. When deciding on next steps, always increase the sample size slowly. There are many, many things that can go wrong when running quantitative tests, so go slowly and make sure that your “success” isn’t just a statistical fluke. #### Unlocking the Power of Data: Introducing Our Experiment Calculator.

They help you figure out the optimal sample size by considering factors like effect size, significance level, and the power you want to achieve. Their use of an online power calculation tool ensures their experiments have enough power to spot effects in their target audience. You just input the **effect size**, **alpha level**, **desired power**, and **variability** into a calculator. These tools help you quickly determine the required sample size for your desired effect size and significance level, ensuring your experiments are properly powered to detect meaningful results. By understanding the key components of power analysis and using tools like the Statsig Calculator, you can optimize your experiments and make the most of your resources. If you're keen to learn more about power analysis and sample size calculations, check out the Statsig documentation and other resources we've linked throughout this blog.

Based on the previous sections, we can make three observations about threshold definition and error control in the SPRT and SBFT: (1) SPRT and SBFT control error rates through the same mechanism, namely threshold adjustment; (2) thresholds need to be defined through simulation methods in both tests if exact error control is desired; and (3) optimal thresholds depend on the model specification.
